summary.text: Plant physiology is the part of botany that studies how plants function, from photosynthesis and respiration to hormones and transpiration.
Its areas include plant chemistry, single cells, interactions among cells, tissues and organs, internal regulation, and response to the environment.
Plant compounds matter to people too, since aspirin is made from salicylic acid and drug companies research plant chemicals for medicines.

items.prompt: Roots take minerals from the soil, but leaves high above need them too. What lets the plant move them there?

options.label: Chlorophyll in the stem carries them upward
Each leaf makes its own, so nothing needs to move
Light stored in the roots pushes them up
Vascular tissue carries them between roots and leaves

items.explain: Minerals from the roots must reach the leaves and nutrients made in the leaves must reach the roots, and plants move them through vascular tissue.

items.prompt: A gardener sees fruit ripen and leaves drop in winter. What helps control both?

options.label: The gas ethylene that the plant produces
Light-sensitive compounds that track night length
The cell wall losing its shape
Trace minerals absorbed through the roots

items.explain: The ripening of fruit and the loss of leaves in winter are controlled in part by the gas ethylene. Night length controls blooming.

items.prompt: Many flowers bloom at just the right time of year. What do they respond to?

options.label: The gas ethylene made by their fruit
The amount of carbon found in the soil
Night length, sensed by light-sensitive compounds
The thickness of their own cell walls

items.explain: Many flowering plants bloom at the appropriate time because light-sensitive compounds respond to the length of the night, called photoperiodism.

items.prompt: A houseplant needs no meals, but a pet cat does. Which feature of plant cells explains the difference?

options.label: A cell wall, which makes nutrients from soil
Chlorophyll, which reacts with light to make nutrients
Hormones, which stand in for food
Vascular tubes, which pull in prey

items.explain: Plant cells contain chlorophyll, which interacts with light so plants manufacture their own nutrients rather than consuming other living things.

items.prompt: A deer is grazing on a plant that cannot run away. How can the plant defend itself?

options.label: By making toxins and foul-tasting or smelling chemicals
By pulling its roots out of the ground
By absorbing more macronutrients
By growing a thicker cell wall around each leaf

items.explain: Because plants cannot move, they defend themselves chemically against herbivores by producing toxins and foul-tasting or smelling chemicals.

items.prompt: A fertilizer label lists 'macro' and 'micro' nutrients. What does the prefix describe?

options.label: The size of the nutrient particles
Whether the nutrient comes from air or soil
How much of the nutrient the plant needs
Whether leaves or roots absorb the nutrient

items.explain: The prefix macro- refers to the quantity needed, not the size of the nutrient particles; micronutrients are needed only in trace amounts.

beats.explain: For both organs to remain living, minerals must be transported to the leaves and manufactured nutrients to the roots.

choices.label: Both would be fine, since each makes all it needs

The leaves would live on, while the roots grew longer

beats.prompt: match each plant part or feature to its job

right.label: Anchor the plant and acquire minerals
Lets plants make their own nutrients using light
Maintains the shape of plant cells

beats.explain: Each part does one specialised job, and together they let the plant feed and hold itself up.

beats.prompt: A plant's flowers bloom at the right time of year. What is the plant responding to?
beats.explain: Light-sensitive compounds respond to the length of the night, a phenomenon called photoperiodism, so many flowering plants bloom at the appropriate time.

choices.label: The length of the night, through light-sensitive compounds
The ethylene gas it releases
choices.feedback: Ethylene helps control fruit ripening and winter leaf loss, not the timing of blooms.

choices.label: The chlorophyll in its cells
choices.feedback: Chlorophyll lets the plant make nutrients from light; it does not time the blooms.

paragraphs.heading: How plants work
paragraphs.text: Plant physiology is the branch of botany that asks how plants function. Its specialists, called plant physiologists, study all the chemical and physical processes of life inside a plant. Their topics include photosynthesis, respiration, nutrition, hormones, tropisms, seed germination, dormancy and transpiration, among others.

paragraphs.heading: From molecules to seasons
paragraphs.text: The field covers many scales of size and time. At the small end are the molecular steps of photosynthesis and the inner diffusion of water, minerals and nutrients. At the large end are the plant's development, the seasons, dormancy and the control of reproduction.

paragraphs.heading: Plant chemistry
paragraphs.text: One major area is plant chemistry. Plants make a wide range of compounds found in no other living things. Since they cannot move, they defend themselves with chemicals, making toxins and foul-tasting or bad-smelling substances against plant-eaters, disease-causing organisms and rival plants. Other compounds help them resist disease, survive drought and get ready for dormancy, or attract pollinators and animals that spread ripe seeds.

paragraphs.heading: Cells, tissues and organs
paragraphs.text: Plant cells differ from animal cells in ways that change how plants behave. A cell wall keeps each cell's shape, and chlorophyll lets the plant use light to make its own nutrients rather than eating other living things. Across the whole plant, roots anchor it and gather minerals from the soil, while leaves catch light to make nutrients. Minerals must travel from roots to leaves and nutrients from leaves to roots, and plants manage this with vascular tissue and other means of transport.

paragraphs.heading: Signals and timing
paragraphs.text: Plant physiologists also study how plants control their own functions. Like animals, plants make hormones, chemicals produced in one part of the plant that signal cells in another part to respond. Many flowering plants bloom at the right time thanks to light-sensitive compounds that react to the length of the night, which is called photoperiodism. The gas ethylene helps control the ripening of fruit and the loss of leaves in winter.

paragraphs.heading: Coping with stress
paragraphs.text: A last area, environmental physiology, looks at how plants respond to their surroundings and how those change. Water loss, shifts in air chemistry or crowding by other plants can alter the way a plant functions. Genetic, chemical and physical factors can all play a part in those changes.

paragraphs.heading: Useful plant compounds
paragraphs.text: Plants are built from the same chemical elements as every other form of life, mainly carbon, oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur. From them, plants still make a huge variety of compounds with special properties. People extract plant pigments for dyes and use plant products to make rubber and biofuel. Aspirin is made from salicylic acid, a plant compound, and morphine and digoxin also come from plants. Drug companies spend billions of dollars a year looking into plant compounds for possible medicines.
